faculty.name: Rachel Bailey
faculty.title: James E. Kirk Professor of Communication, Director of Doctoral Studies
faculty.bio:
Dr. Rachel L. Bailey is the James E. Kirk Professor of Communication at Florida State University. Her research examines human interactions with and via media and is rooted in biological and evolutionary perspectives including embodied, situated cognition and motivated cognition. She commonly uses this lens to investigate how media are influential in important social and health contexts, such as health perceptions, food choice, substance use, and vicarious trauma of mediated violence.
Dr. Bailey’s research is especially relevant in the fields of media psychology, health communication, and media processes and effects. Her work is published in leading journals in the field including
Journal of Communication, Communication Research, Communication Monographs, Human Communication Research
,
Media Psychology, Journal of Media Psychology,
Health Communication,
and
Journal of Health Communication
. She also has published in interdisciplinary journals including
Appetite, Journal of Nutrition Education & Behavior, Cognition & Emotion
,
Motivation & Emotion
,
Physiology & Behavior, Health Environments Research & Design,
and C
riminal Justice & Behavior
. She recently co-edited the
The DeGruyter Handbook of Media Psychology
, a comprehensive look at the field and its current directions.
Prior to joining the academy, Dr. Bailey worked in the advertising research industry at a small biometric research firm exclusively contracted to Disney Media Networks.

faculty.name: Sindy Chapa
faculty.title: Professor & Director of the Hispanic Marketing Center
faculty.bio:
Dr. Sindy Chapa is an
FSU School of Communication
Associate Professor and the Director for the School’s
Center for Hispanic Marketing Communication (HMC)
.
With over 10 years of teaching experience, Chapa has taught marketing courses in the U.S., Mexico and Chile.  Previously she worked as an Assistant Professor and Associate Director of the
Center for the Study of Latino Media & Markets
at
The School of Journalism & Mass Communication
at Texas State University (TSU) since 2008.
While at TSU, Chapa served as organizing committee co-chair for two
Assessing The State of Spanish-Language & Latino-Oriented Media International Conferences
.  Global scholars from universities in Barcelona, Colombia, Mexico and Puerto Rico as well as the U.S. gather annually to present their research work, findings, and theories.  The conference typically covers topics about marketing communication, telecommunication policies, media adoption and culture, among others.
At FSU, Chapa plans to continue her research, which focuses on the effect of advertising strategies on Latino consumers.  She will be teaching Hispanic Marketing Communication in the fall semester.
Chapa earned a Ph.D. in International Business from University of Texas-Pan American, M.B.A. from the University of St. Thomas in Texas and a B.A. in Mass Media Communications with a minor in television and art design from Valle Del Bravo University in Mexico.

faculty.name: Russell Clayton
faculty.title: Distinguished and Endowed Provost McKenzie Professor
faculty.bio:
Dr. Russell B. Clayton is the Distinguished and Endowed Provost McKenzie Professor at Florida State University, where he is a Professor in the School of Communication and Director of the
Cognition and Emotion Lab.
He earned his B.S. in psychology and M.A. in health psychology from Texas State University and his Ph.D. from the University of Missouri, with a focus in health and strategic communication. His research centers on media psychology, health communication, and psychophysiological methods, with a particular emphasis on evaluating and optimizing persuasive health messages aimed at preventing and reducing substance use—including drug, alcohol, tobacco, and non-tobacco nicotine use—among young adults.
Dr. Clayton’s research program has been supported by more than $3.4 million in competitive funding from federal (NIH/NCI), state (FDOT), field, and university foundation sources. He has authored more than 45 peer-reviewed publications in flagship communication, psychology, medicine, and health journals and serves on the editorial boards of nine leading communication journals.
Dr. Clayton teaches undergraduate and graduate courses in media and communication studies and has received three university-level teaching awards, including the
University Distinguished Teaching award
, the university’s highest honor for teaching, presented annually to a single faculty member.

faculty.name: Katherine R. Dale
faculty.title: Associate Professor
faculty.bio:
Dr. Katherine Dale (Ph.D., The Ohio State University, 2015) is an Assistant Professor in the School of Communication. Her research interests include positive media psychology, intergroup interactions, and media effects. She is most interested in exploring the ways that media can positively affect our attitudes, behavior, and well-being. Her research has been published in journals such as
Journal of Communication
,
Mass Communication and Society
, and
Journal of Media Psychology
.
Research interests: Positive Media Psychology, Media Effects; Intergroup Interaction

faculty.name: Arienne Ferchaud
faculty.title: Associate Professor
faculty.bio:
Dr. Arienne Ferchaud (Ph.D., Pennsylvania State University, 2018) is an Assistant Professor in the School of Communication.
Dr. Ferchaud’s research focuses broadly on emerging media entertainment from a media psychology perspective. She is interested in how new media technologies change the way users engage with entertainment content. She has a special interest in narrative theory and how new modes of storytelling change how we perceive stories. Her work has been published in journals such as
Computers in Human Behavior,
Journal of Gaming and Virtual Worlds,
Human Communication Research,
and
Imagination, Cognition and Personality
, and her research has been presented at both national and international conferences. She is also the author of
Binge and Bingeability: The Antecedents and Consequences of Binge Watching Behavior
.
Research interests: Media Effects; Emerging Media Entertainment; Narrative Theory

faculty.name: Braidyn Lazenby
faculty.title: Assistant Professor
faculty.bio:
Hi there!
My name is Braidyn Lazenby. I am thrilled to be an Assistant Professor here at FSU. My research interests include interpersonal health communication. More specifically, I specialize in how people navigate difficult conversations about health with healthcare providers, friends, family members, and romantic partners. I am passionate about translating health communication scholarship into tangible resources for the broader public. Some of my previous research has focused on stigmatized conditions, eating disorders, and fad diets, among many other things. My research can be found in journals such as
Health Communication
,
Qualitative Health Research
,
Social Science and Medicine
, and more. I love chatting about health communication, so feel free to stop by my office, email me, or check out my work through my Google Scholar profile here:
Braidyn Lazenby – Google Scholar Profile
In my spare time I love trying new restaurants, finding live music, and engaging with the local wildlife here in Florida. I am also an avid sports fan and enjoy cheering on all of my teams in all of the sports. I have enough spirit to span Bama, Texas, and now FSU.
Go Noles!

faculty.name: Stephen McDowell
faculty.title: Assistant Provost, John H. Phipps Professor of Communication
faculty.bio:
Stephen D. McDowell serves as the Assistant Provost for International Initiatives at Florida State University (2018 – present).   He also serves as the John H. Phipps Professor in the School of Communication at Florida State University (2006-present).  He served as Department Chair (2002-2013), Associate Dean (2013-2021), and Interim Dean of the College of Communication and Information at FSU (August 2021- June 2023).
His research and teaching interests address news, and communication technology and  policy in South Asia and North America. He has co-edited, with Sahana Udupa,
Media as Politics in South
Asia (Routledge, 2017), co-authored, with Phillip Steinberg and Tami Tomasello,
Managing The Infosphere: Governance, Technology, and Cultural Practice in Motion
(Temple University Press, 2007), and authored,
Globalization, Liberalization and Policy Change: A Political Economy of India’s Communications Sector
(St. Martin’s, 1997).
McDowell has held fellowships with the Canadian federal Department of Communications in Ottawa, Canada (1987-1989), with the Shastri Indo-Canadian Institute in New Delhi, India (1989-1990), and a Congressional Fellowship supported by the American Political Science Association in Washington, D.C. (1994-1995).
Research interests: Media Policy; New Media; International Communication; Internet Governance; South Asian Media; Intercultural Communication

faculty.name: Elizabeth Ray
faculty.title: Assistant Professor
faculty.bio:
Elizabeth Ray is an Assistant Professor at Florida State University, where she researches and teaches crisis, risk, resilience, and strategic communication. Her work examines how people interpret uncertainty and adversity, and how communication can support their response and recovery. She has studied how audiences understand risk information during extreme weather events, how they judge the credibility of AI-generated crisis messages, and how trauma-informed online interventions support resilience.
Her research appears in
Health Communication
, the
International Journal of Strategic Communication
,
Weather, Climate, and Society
, and the
Journal of Public Relations Education
.
Elizabeth’s academic work grows out of a career in practice. She worked as a television news reporter across Florida, including in Jacksonville, Panama City, and Gainesville, and later served as Communications and Marketing Director for a statewide hospitality trade association. She has also contributed to communications committees for VISIT FLORIDA, the Council of State Restaurant Associations, and the Florida Public Relations Association’s Capital Chapter. In the classroom, she draws on this experience to show students how strategic communication works with real audiences and real stakes.
Outside of work, Elizabeth enjoys time with her three sons, Elijah, Isaiah, and Caleb, and her husband, Whitney, a phenomenal cook.

faculty.name: Richard Waters
faculty.title: Associate Professor
faculty.bio:
Richard D. Waters, Ph.D., is a public relations educator and scholar whose research examines strategic communication, nonprofit communication, relationship management, and digital engagement. The author of over 115 peer-reviewed journal articles and book chapters, he earned his Ph.D. in Mass Communication from the University of Florida in 2007. Waters has published extensively on stakeholder relationships, fundraising and nonprofit communication, social media strategy, and public relations pedagogy. Waters is the editor of
Public Relations in the Nonprofit Sector: Theory and Practice
and co-editor of
Coming out of the Closet: Exploring LGBT Issues in Strategic Communication with Theory and Research.
He has authored numerous articles in journals including
Public Relations Review
,
Journal of Public Relations Research
,
Journal of Public Relations
Education,
and
Journalism & Mass Communication Educator
. His teaching and scholarship frequently explore the intersections of ethics, crisis communication, and emerging communication technologies in organizational settings. Waters has also worked with nonprofit organizations and corporations on strategic communication initiatives and community engagement efforts.
Research interests: Public Relations, Nonprofit Communication, Fundraising Theory
Publications & Research: Select articles published while at Florida State University:
Waters, R. D., Ray, E. C. & Rolle, E. (2026).

faculty.name: Jessica Wendorf Muhamad
faculty.title: Director of Undergraduate Studies | Director PEAKS Research Laboratory | Associate Professor
faculty.bio:
Jessica Wendorf Muhamad, Ph.D. is an Associate Professor of Communication in the College of Communication and Information at Florida State University, where she serves as Director of Undergraduate Studies. She is also Director of the PEAKS laboratory (Participatory, Experientially-based Applied Knowledge for Social Change), which focuses on developing, through action research, evidence-based interventions for complex social issues.
As a prevention scientist, Dr. Wendorf Muhamad examines how enacted, entertainment-education experiences—including game-based interventions—shape attitudes and behavior at the individual, interpersonal, and community levels. Her research program (1) develops culturally relevant, experientially based health interventions through community-engaged, participatory design; (2) examines how prosocial narrative, embedded within experiential learning, influences attitudes and behaviors around health and social issues while attending to the interpersonal and nonverbal dynamics through which these experiences are communicated; and (3) extends beyond intervention design to a broader account of adoptability and sustainability, examining implementation climate and the social determinants that shape whether interventions take hold within communities and organizations.

faculty.name: Yin Yang
faculty.title: Assistant Professor
research_areas: Health Communication (Women’s Health, Stigma and Health, Health Inequities)
faculty.bio:
Yin Yang (Ph.D., The Pennsylvania State University, 2024) is an assistant professor in the School of Communication at Florida State University. Her research examines how media messages affect recipients’ beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors in health and environmental contexts, with a focus on narrative persuasion and emotions. She is particularly interested in the messaging efforts to promote awareness of and engagement with overlooked or/and stigmatized issues (e.g., menstrual health, mental health, health inequities, climate justice).
Dr. Yang’s research can be found in journals such as
Human Communication Research
,
Mass Communication and Society
,
Health Communication
,
Environmental Communication
. Her work has been awarded the Article of the Year from the AEJMC Communicating Science, Health, Environment, and Risk division. She has received support for research from the Organization for Feminist Research on Gender and Communication and the Arthur W. Page Center for Integrity in Public Communications.
Dr. Yang teaches communication research methods and social marketing in the School of Communication.
Research interests: Media Effects (Narrative Persuasion, Emotions); Health Communication (Women’s Health, Stigma and Health, Health Inequities); Environmental Communication

faculty.name: Annie Zhang
faculty.title: Assistant Professor
faculty.bio:
Annie Zhang (Ph.D., University of Michigan) is an assistant professor in science communication in the School of Communication at Florida State University. Her research explores how digital spaces and emerging technologies shape the public communication and understanding of science, health, and environmental issues. With a background as both a science journalist and a chemist, she bring an interdisciplinary perspective that informs her work. Her research aims to build positive and meaningful relationships between scientists and the public and promote evidence-based communication strategies that not only enhance public understanding of, but also inspire public engagement and interest in science.
Dr. Zhang’s research has been published in interdisiciplinary peer-reviewed journals such as
Cell, Science Communication,
New Media & Society, Social Media & Society,
and
Information, Communication, and Society
. Her work has been supported by the National Science Foundation.
Research interests: Science Communication, Media Effects, Public Engagement with Science, Social Media

faculty.name: Pengfei Zhao
faculty.title: Assistant Professor
faculty.bio:
Pengfei Zhao (Ph.D., Cornell University) is an assistant professor in communication & AI in the School of Communication at Florida State University. Her research focuses on the psychological, interpersonal, and socio-technical processes and effects of emerging media and technology, such as social media and artificial intelligence (AI). Dr. Zhao develops theory-driven and evidence-based interventions to reduce online harms, foster civil and constructive discourses, and improve digital literacy. Based on her past work on the interpersonal and relational processes within community technologies, Dr. Zhao’s current research spans two key themes: 1) understanding how moral behaviors from humans and AI shape community norms and dynamics in digital spaces, and 2) developing AI-powered and community-driven interventions that reduce online harms and facilitate prosocial behaviors and norms.
Dr. Zhao’s work has been published in interdisciplinary peer-reviewed journals, including
PNAS Nexus
,
Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication
,
Current Opinion in Psychology
,
Computers in Human Behavior
,
Review of Education Research
, and
Journal of Adolescent Health
.
You can find more information on my
personal website
.
Research interests: Technology and well-being; Human-AI interaction; AI for community governance; AI and morality; Online toxicity intervention; Computer-mediated communication
